organizingIdeas.title: Text Forms and Structures
organizingIdeas.statement: Identifying and applying text forms and structures improves understanding of content, literary style, and our rich language traditions.

guidingQuestions.question: How can the organization of ideas and information support the sharing of messages?

outcomes.outcome: Students examine ways that messages can be organized and presented for different purposes.

knowledge.text: Messages can be shared for different reasons (purposes), including to learn, have fun, and stay safe.
Messages can depict ideas and information that are imaginary (fiction) or real (non-fiction).
Messages can be shared digitally or non-digitally through
Messages can be shared in a variety of forms, including
Stories, both real and imaginary, can follow a structure, including
Environmental print includes signs, symbols, and words.
Books and other forms of print are organized in specific ways (concepts of print):
items: A book has a title and an author.
Print is read from left to right and top to bottom with a return sweep.
Each print word represents one spoken word when read aloud.
Sentences are made up of words.
Words are separated by spaces in sentences.
Punctuation marks can signal the end of a sentence.

understanding.text: Ideas and information can be organized by purpose, form, or structure.

organizingIdeas.title: Oral Language
organizingIdeas.statement: Listening and speaking form the foundation for literacy development and improve communication, collaboration, and respectful mutual understanding.

guidingQuestions.question: In what ways can listening and speaking be applied to develop oral communication?

outcomes.outcome: Students develop listening and speaking skills through sharing stories and information.

knowledge.text: Stories that are shared through listening and speaking (oral traditions) can be handed down from generation to generation.
Kinship involves belonging and relationships.
Oral stories are highly valued in many communities.
Communities may have special rules (protocols) about how, when, or with whom stories are shared.

understanding.text: Oral traditions can provide opportunities to learn and think about kinship.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Practise listening and speaking skills through sharing oral stories.
Recognize kinship in a variety of oral stories.
Discuss special rules (protocols) about how, when, or with whom stories are shared.

Speakers can indicate differences in character, key ideas, and events through changes in volume, tone, and pace.

understanding.text: Listening and speaking can be used to share messages in a variety of situations.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Examine verbal and non-verbal language that is appropriate for a variety of situations.
Adjust verbal or non-verbal language according to a variety of situations.

organizingIdeas.title: Vocabulary
organizingIdeas.statement: Communication and comprehension are improved by understanding word meaning and structures.

guidingQuestions.question: How can vocabulary and morphological awareness work together to increase knowledge of words?

outcomes.outcome: Students analyze word formation and meaning.

knowledge.text: Vocabulary development includes learning (tier 2) words that are
items: useful and may be encountered in the future

knowledge.text: Vocabulary development includes some academic words (tier 3 words) from read alouds and texts.
A synonym is a word that has a similar meaning to another word.
An antonym is a word that has the opposite meaning of another word.

understanding.text: Learning new words improves comprehension and communication.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Confirm word meanings in a variety of ways.
Identify the meaning of tier 2 words and use them in sentences.
Use tier 3 words in discussions.
Recognize that words can be replaced with synonyms.

knowledge.text: A base is the main morpheme (the smallest unit of a word that holds meaning) in a word.
Suffixes are morphemes located at the ending of words.
Adding the suffix <s> or <es> to the ending of a word can indicate more than one (plural).
Adding the suffix <ed> to the ending of a word indicates something has already happened (changes the tense).
A compound word is formed when two individual words are put together to make a new word.
The meaning of a compound word can be similar to or different from the two individual words that were combined to form the word.

understanding.text: Word meanings can change by adding or removing morphemes.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Identify words according to their base.
Recognize suffixes in oral or written language.
Add or remove suffixes to make words plural or singular.
Add or remove suffixes to change the tense of words.
Recognize compound words.
Describe changes in meaning that occur when two words are combined to form a compound word.

organizingIdeas.title: Phonological Awareness
organizingIdeas.statement: Foundational literacy is supported by the ability to identify and manipulate sounds in oral language.

guidingQuestions.question: How does the manipulation of sound in oral language support phonological awareness?

outcomes.outcome: Students manipulate sounds in words in oral language.

knowledge.text: A series of words or phrases that begin with the same sound can be combined for humorous effect (alliteration) (e.g., tongue twisters).

understanding.text: Sounds in words (phonemes) can be repeated for effect.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Generate alliterative words.
Generate alliterative phrases.

knowledge.text: Words that rhyme can have more than one syllable.

understanding.text: Rhyming words can be present in a variety of oral language contexts.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Generate rhyming words that have up to three syllables.
Recall simple songs or poems that contain words that rhyme.

knowledge.text: Compound words can be separated into two individual words.
Words can be separated into syllables.
Words can be separated into sounds.
Sounds can be identified at the beginning, in the middle, or at the ending of spoken words.

understanding.text: Separating words into syllables or phonemes (segmentation) supports the ability to hear and manipulate sounds in words.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Identify individual words in compound words.
Identify syllables in words that have three or more syllables.
Segment the sounds of words containing up to five phonemes.

knowledge.text: Two separate words can be blended to form a new word (compound word).
Syllables can be blended to form new words.
Sounds (phonemes) can be blended to form words.

understanding.text: Words can be formed by blending words, parts of words, or sounds.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Blend two words to form compound words.
Blend syllables in words that have two to three syllables.
Blend sounds in words that have up to five phonemes.

knowledge.text: Sounds can be added to the beginning, middle, or ending of words.
Sounds can be deleted from the beginning, middle, or ending of words.
Sounds can be substituted for different sounds at the beginning, middle, or ending of words.

understanding.text: Sounds in words can be added, deleted, or substituted (manipulated).

skillsAndProcedures.text: Recognize the position of letters in words.
Add sounds to the beginning, middle, or ending of words.
Delete sounds from the beginning, middle, or ending of words.
Substitute one sound for another in one-syllable words.

organizingIdeas.title: Phonics
organizingIdeas.statement: Foundational literacy is supported by understanding relationships between sounds in oral language and the letters that represent them.

guidingQuestions.question: How can understanding relationships between sounds and letters (phonics) increase knowledge of words?

outcomes.outcome: Students recognize and analyze letters and sounds in words.

knowledge.text: The English alphabet consists of a set of 26 letters that represent sounds.
Letters can be upper case or lower case.

understanding.text: Letters represent sounds in words.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Recognize both upper case and lower case letters of the alphabet fluently.
Distinguish between letters that are consonants and letters that are vowels.
Make connections between letters and sounds in words.

knowledge.text: There is a relationship between written letters (graphemes) and the sounds they represent (phonemes).
Two or more letters can represent a single sound.
Letters in words can be silent.
Some letters have variable pronunciations.
A vowel that is followed by <r> can make a new sound (e.g., ti-ger, turn, and bird).

understanding.text: Letter combinations represent units of sound within a word.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Associate sounds to letters and letter sequences.
Experiment with letters, sounds, and words to create new words.
Read one- to two-syllable words that include the 60 most frequent letter-sound correspondences.
Recognize and use long and short vowel sounds in words.
Read and write consonant sounds in the beginning, middle, and ending of words, using the letters that represent them.

Identify short vowel sounds in words and identify the letters that represent them.
Identify long vowel sounds in words and identify the letters that represent them.
Recognize how the letter <r> can influence the vowel sound.

organizingIdeas.title: Fluency
organizingIdeas.statement: Comprehension and literary appreciation are improved by the ability to read a range of texts accurately, automatically, and with expression.

guidingQuestions.question: How does reading prosody (expression) support fluency?

outcomes.outcome: Students apply accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression in the development of fluency.

knowledge.text: Letters can be recognized quickly and accurately.
Sounds in words can be blended quickly and accurately.
Words consisting of three sounds (three phonemes) can be blended quickly and accurately.

understanding.text: Fluency involves the ability to decode new words with accuracy and at an appropriate rate.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Identify all 26 letters of the alphabet quickly and accurately.
Blend sounds in words with speed and accuracy to decode unfamiliar words.

knowledge.text: High-frequency words are common words that occur often in written language.
Some words that appear often in print cannot be decoded and must be read by sight (e.g., the).

understanding.text: Fluency involves the ability to recognize high-frequency words with accuracy and at an appropriate rate.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Read 125 high-frequency words automatically.
Read 125 high-frequency words in sentences and texts.

knowledge.text: Phrased reading sounds like spoken language.
Fluent reading includes stopping at periods and pausing at commas.

items: loud and soft stresses of words
raising the voice as a response to question marks

understanding.text: Fluent and phrased reading can increase the ability to comprehend written messages.

skillsAndProcedures.text: Read phrases smoothly, taking punctuation into consideration.

organizingIdeas.title: Comprehension
organizingIdeas.statement: Text comprehension is supported by applying varied strategies and processes and by considering both particular contexts and universal themes.

outcomes.outcome: Students investigate meaning communicated in texts.

knowledge.text: Texts that are listened to can contain more formal or complex language than everyday language.
Responses to messages listened to in texts include
items: pictures with a few words or sentences

organizingIdeas.title: Writing
organizingIdeas.statement: Ideas and information can be articulated accurately and imaginatively through the use of writing processes and an understanding of the author’s craft.

guidingQuestions.question: How can writing be used to communicate meaning?

outcomes.outcome: Students create messages through the application of writing processes.

knowledge.text: Processes that can be used to support writing messages include
Planning involves thinking or talking about
items: why you are writing a message (purpose)
who will be reading the message (audience)

Editing involves correcting errors in spelling, grammar, and punctuation.
Messages can be created by individuals or groups.

understanding.text: Ideas and information can be shared through written messages.

organizingIdeas.title: Conventions
organizingIdeas.statement: Understanding grammar, spelling, and punctuation makes it easier to communicate clearly, to organize thinking, and to use language for desired effects.

guidingQuestions.question: How do the functions of conventions support literacy development?

outcomes.outcome: Students examine and apply use of grammar, spelling, and punctuation in oral and written language.
